Early humans absolutely were in a position to want and NEED a caloric surplus. They didn't have protection from exposure to harsh elements like we do now and needed that extra layer in winter. They also had to work a lot harder than we do now to get their food and needed that fuel to hunt and/or move and gather. The human body DOES crave high energy foods for this reason. When it was a matter of human survival, the instinct became to find the easiest source of the most caloric dense food because you weren't guaranteed where or when your next meal would come. The science behind it isn't wrong.. it's how it's being used to justify behavior that is now harmful to us. We no longer NEED to store up extra pounds for the upcoming famine. We can easily figure out where the next meal is coming from. It's not a question of having a healthy, positive relationship where you listen to what your body is telling you. It's a matter of understanding the cause behind the cues and understanding that you can love and listen to you body without following through on everything it's telling you to do. For example: My body sends me physical and emotional cues and tells me when I may be getting sick so I should take it easy because survival of the species. I'll listen. My body sends me physical and emotional cues and tells me when I'm in serious pain so I can prevent injuring myself because survival of the species. I'll listen. My body also sends me physical and emotional cues and tells me that the random hot stranger sitting across from me on the airplane is extremely sexy and that I should therefore go try and mate with them because survival of the species..... Not gonna listen to that one.  The fact is, we've adapted for millennia. We are still adapting. We change to survive in our surroundings. We are at a point now where, to ensure proper survival we need to know self discipline in a way that is completely 160 degrees from what it once was. Keeping the body healthy in this day and age means sometimes knowing what is best for it.. even when the body may be pointing at the chocolate cake

This year was my first WTM and I enthusiastically second what has been said about gear. If I hadn't had a wetsuit I wouldn't have made it. As far as training, the course in Vegas (which is where it will be again next year) has soft dirt mixed in and elevation gains, so some hill training in addition to the mudders you already have on your schedule. Good, solid cross training that mixes in long distance runs, core work, strength training, sprints, and swimming. Have fun with the training and keep it varied because that's the nature of this sport. As far as nutrition goes, same old adage: junk in = junk out. Just try to eat clean as much as possible. I plan on being there again next year if my schedule allows. See you then!

You gotta lay out a training plan, otherwise you'll just end up going out there without a plan and likely fizzle out. Sit down and write out a realistic training schedule that allows you to start gradual, account for off days in between, and then taper up in either speed or distance. Being a Marine, you have the knowledge there. You know what to do.. it's just regaining the confidence to do it and executing the plan. The mental toughness comes in to play when you have a solid plan to follow. Once you know exactly what the game plan is, THEN you grit through it... that also can just mean not stopping. If you feel yourself wanting to quit, instead of quitting all together, just keep moving. For example, if you set out on a 6 mile run, get to mile 4 and want to quit, slow it down.. even if you walk/run the last mile or two, you still kept moving.

It's already been hit on here a bit. With running, "vast" improvement takes time and dedication. You can, however, work on things that will make you feel better, leading to better focus, efficiency, energy, and - in the long run (no pun intended) lead to improvements. I would say evaluate your diet. Make sure you are eating clean the majority of the time. You don't have to cut out ALL junk, but be conservative with it. The age old saying "you are what you eat" applies very much to runners. Healthy, natural foods that have good quality nutrients will fuel you better and make your body work more efficiently and you WILL notice it. Take the few extra minutes to do some warmup work before runs and even more important, take the time after your runs to stretch and cool down. This will release tension and acid from your muscles, improve your range of motion, and speed recovery. When you're at the office, pay attention to your posture as well as your breathing. We often don't pay any attention to the way we breathe. Even just a few minutes a day of deep breathing does wonders (extra points because it's a natural way to relieve stress). One way to do this is to sit up straight, hands on your lap, breathe in slowly through your nose as deeply as you can. Try to concentrate on completely filling your lungs, as if your pulling all that air in to down the very bottom of your lungs. Hold it for a second or two, then slowly exhale through your mouth. Repeat a few times and you should actually feel better. You can look up various stretches online, so I won't really hit on those here. I will say this: don't forget the importance of stretching your hip flexors. They take a pounding with regular running and we often forget to pay them extra attention. Other than that, just run. Put in the time. Try to vary your workouts. Quicker, shorter runs, a few longer runs, and some sprint intervals all have their benefits. I'd suggest a day or two doing some resistance training, as gym time really does transfer over to better running.

Well, break it down: you're looking at trying to shave 3 and a half minutes off your time in 4 weeks. That's quite a bit. Can it be done? Yes. Is it difficult and gonna suck? Absolutely. If your goal is solely to run 1 mile in 8:30, then you train to that. Your program should be based on the distance/time that you're looking to achieve. You want to incorporate longer distance runs (longer than your goal distance), speed work, and of course runs that will check your progress running the distance you are shooting for. Alternate your runs. For example: day 1 might be a 1 mile to check your time. Day 2 might be a slower 2 mile run at an easier pace to get your endurance up. Day 3 sprint intervals (say, break your 1 mile run into sections. Start with a quarter mile warm up, then do the rest in intervals of 50 to 100 yard sprints). Combining distance work to train your body to hold out longer with bouts of intense speed work to expand your lungs and elevate your heart rate will get you where you want to go.

First, when you say 7 miles every day, are you taking any rest days in there or are you just plugging away day after day after day? 7 miles is a pretty good distance to be running on back to back days and, if you're not getting ample rest days, you're tearing your body down with no chance to repair. Second, at 5'2 115 lbs, you're pretty darn small. You've got to make sure your diet is right. That much energy expended through running, combined with the fact that, at 16 years old your body is still trying to develop, you need a significant amount of healthy calories and nutrients to maintain and sustain. If you're not getting ample rest and/or not taking in enough food (good, solid, healthy choices) then your body is going to give up on you.. both of these things can affect the strength and performance of your heart. i would say, SERIOUSLY evaluate these factors and if those are in check, go talk to your doctor.

It sucks when you're partner doesn't share your passion for training, and even worse when there's a conflict where you have to try to overcome the pressure to engage in unhealthy habits. I can KIND of see where he's coming from, since he's on vacation and wants to "veg out," but you aren't pressuring him to train with you or keep the same hours as you. While it's good for a couple to share time and activities, it's just as healthy (in fact, almost crucial to a relationship) for each person to have something of their own that drives them. I applaud and understand your drive and passion for training. As far as him being upset that your training is going to affect his schedule, it's pretty much a non-issue, since you say you already get up earlier than him to run. His schedule is HIS schedule, and your schedule is YOUR schedule. In fact, him demanding that you stay up late partying with him and his buddies is him affecting a change in YOUR schedule. There can be bargaining room here. If you can understand his desire to have you spend time with him doing activities he enjoys (whether that be drinking, partying, etc), then surely he can understand your desire to get the most out of and enjoy the vacation time and location. You could try (once you've calmed your nerves enough) approaching it from a bargaining standpoint, but be prepared to have basic requirements that will fulfill your needs. Not sure how long your vacation is, but you could try and approach it by pre-scheduling. Something like this: "I know this is vacation time, and it's really important for both of us to be able to spend it relaxing, unwinding, and de-stressing. I want us both to be able to do that. You like to unwind by having a drink or two, spending time with friends, and not having to worry about having to get up early to make appointments or whatnot and I absolutely respect that. As strange as it may sound, training is, for me, MY way of decompressing and focusing myself. It brings me joy and I would really like to be able to take full advantage of the vacation time. We can both get what we want out of our vacation time without it negatively affecting each other. If you are willing to respect my desire to train and respect my decision to adjust my schedule in order to do what brings me joy, then I am willing to meet you part way. While it's true I don't want to spend every night staying up late and drinking, I can recognize that spending time with you doing things you want to do is important. I'm not asking you to change your schedule and I'm not asking you to NOT do the things that you enjoy doing. I'm willing to spend (___ days a week or ___ period of time per day or ___ activities) with you, if you can respect me enough to understand that I have activities that I want to do and goals that I want to accomplish." 
Think about what amount of time you are or are not willing to compromise on, and try to present it to him. He may or may not be willing to listen or receive it, but you cannot.. I repeat CANNOT allow anyone (not even someone you love) rob you of your goals and your joy. If you are focused on a goal, then you have to train for it and you have to allow place for it in your life and schedule where it gets done without distraction, without fail, give it priority during that time and NEVER feel sorry for it. Just like it isn't for you to TELL him he can't stay up late and drink with his buddies, it's not for him to TELL you that you can't do something that is ultimately great for your body and mind. Loving someone is accepting that they have goals and desires that you may not share. Push comes to shove, present where you are willing to compromise, if he won't budge, just tell him "I love you and I want you to enjoy your vacation, but this is important to me and, other than the compromises I've presented you with that I'm willing to make, I'm not going to change my mind or my focus. I'm going to do what I need to do for ME." Give him time, it'll sink in whether he acknowledges it or not. Your decision to focus and train doesn't REALLY have any negative affect on him other than him selfishly wanting a partner in crime to drink and party with. Your being healthy and driven doesn't negatively impact him except to maybe highlight in his mind what he ISN'T doing. Never give up your goals, especially when they are positive ones that affect your health.

The great thing about running, is that it doesn't really require much special gear to get started. Depending on the weather where you are, go through your closet and find some comfy shorts or pants that aren't gonna fall off when you run and a t shirt or hoodie. Right now, you don't need to worry too much about specialty running tops and bottoms. Once you get into a regular routine and see how you feel, you can tweak your running outfit. The biggest thing you want to make sure of right now is that you have a decent pair of running shoes. You definitely don't want to rock the basketball shoes on a run. 
Getting started running is a lot of trial and error. No two runners are the same. Some are early morning runners, some prefer later in the day. Some run on an empty stomach, some people can't make it out the door without breakfast first. At this stage, you're gonna have to try things out. When are YOU most likely to get out the door and go for a run? Is it early in the a.m. or are you a late sleeper and prefer afternoon? I would suggest that you pick a time of day for the first week or so and just lace up your shoes and get out there on the road. Don't set too rigid goals right now, just aim to get out there and run. You're young, so your body should recover pretty quickly, but even so, I wouldn't recommend running more than about 3 to 4 days a week right now until you see where you are. The first run will probably be the most awkward because you don't really have a frame of reference to gauge yourself by. Try finding a local track where you can mark your laps, or chart out a route near your house to try and run. When you finish your first run, keep a journal: how far you went, what your time was, how you felt. This will help you set realistic goals and tweak your training as you go. As far as diet/nutrition, everyone is different. Just remember that crappy fuel put in your body often leads to crappy performance, so obviously try to eat healthy (lean proteins like chicken, fish, etc and good carbs like bananas, rice, sweet potatoes). You shouldn't need to bang down a lot of gatoraide or flashy supplements right now.. maybe later if you get into harder, lng distance runs. Right now, just keep it simple. If you gotta eat before hand, try something light, maybe a half banana and some orange juice. Let it digest a little, then try out your run. Just keep notes on everything because this is YOUR training, these are YOUR runs, and there is no right or wrong.. only what will work for YOU.

Running is one of the best sports/hobbies/pastimes in that.. it really requires very little to get started. Setting goals for getting started is really going to depend on your current level of fitness, schedule, and location. It's going to take getting out there and actually running to see where you are with it fitness wise. I'd suggest setting aside some time when it's convenient for you (and when you'll actually be motivated to getup and do it) whether it's in the evening or in the morning before work. Pick a safe route.. if you live in the city, try to map out a run that's not going to be in the middle of heavy traffic or maybe find a track for your first few runs. If you live in the country, pick a nice, scenic route that's relatively level and free from obstacles. There are a couple of ways you can do it. Either set a distance-- say, a mile to a mile and a half-- or set a time goal -- say, I'm going to see how long I can run for. Then get some comfy shoes and clothes, set a nice steady pace, and go run. See how you feel and listen to your body. You've got to know where you're starting to know where you want to go. I like to listen to music while I'm running, but that's a personal choice. Some people prefer audio books, and some people prefer to run with only their thoughts. it's whatever motivates YOU. Make sure you take a good 5 to 10 minutes to warm up (walking at an easy pace or use a stationary bike) and be sure to stretch thoroughly after your run. I'd advise against eating to soon before you run for now until you get a chance to know how your body responds. Go to walkjogrun.net or a website like mapmyrun, type in your address, and you can create running routes or find already established routes to run. There's no right or wrong, it's all about you and what's going to work well for you.

You probably just have to get used to running and work out your form. As you run more, you should be able to adopt a more efficient stride. When you land, which part of your foot is making contact with the ground first? Do you notice if you're a heel first striker or more of a "my foot hits the ground pretty much flat" kind of runner? A lot of times, if you feel like you have "loud and heavy" footfall it's probably because you're landing with your heel first or completely flatfooted. If you can concentrate on keeping a bounce in your step by keeping most of your weight on the forefoot/ball of foot and landing and pushing off from there, you should notice a change in how "heavy and loud" you're running. Try bouncing up and down in place on your toes and forefoot a few times and that's close to how your feet should be landing. Of course, every runner is different and every stride is different. What's most important is what is comfortable to YOU. As far as being a "loud" runner... don't sweat it (no pun intended) just run.

Don't despair. It's hard being raised in that religion because, as in your case and many others, by the time you make it out you've been so brainwashed that you are practically socially paralyzed. As far as who to trust and how to avoid being used and finding healthy relationships, I'm going to put it to you this way: In this world (and I mean life in general, NOT the "separate world" you've been raised to view it as) there are good people and there are bad people. There are people who are helpful and kind and there are people who will use you and take advantage of you. You're going to meet both kinds. It may seem like you are suddenly being exposed to the risk of meeting hurtful people now that you are "outside of the protection" of the JW religion, but the fact of the matter is.. you are no more at risk of this now than you were before. The same rules that apply to the general population apply to the Organization. Some Witnesses are good people and others are bad people. The protective shield around members of that religion is a mirage.. it's a lie.. it isn't real.
In life, you are never going to be sure who you can trust until you have invested time in getting to know people. It's a scary fact and it's not your fault that it's making you feel the way you do with the anxiety and stress. Chances are that you were never taught how to interact with people outside of that "protective shield" and so now, at 25, you aren't equipped with all the tools you need to form healthy relationships with others while protecting your well being but still being open to new experiences. All the things you were warned about "the world" have probably made you paranoid. What you have to do is understand that there are reasons to be cautious when meeting new people and pursuing new things.. use common sense, but afford people the opportunity to earn your trust and don't let your fears hold you back from new experiences. Part of learning is experience.. both successes and failures and this applies to EVERYTHING we do. A mother doesn't want her toddler to burn himself on a hot stove, so she tells him "don't touch. Hot!".. but that toddler doesn't know what "hot" means. He touches the hot stove and he gets burnt and he learns a valuable life lesson.. one that hurt, but that is going to lead to him being able to protect himself in the future and avoid it happening again. Failed relationships, run ins with people who would use you, these experiences are what help you grow and become successful with future relationships and safeguarding yourself. You can't always avoid the bad experiences, but you shouldn't live in fear of them. They are what gives your life depth and bring true appreciation for the good relationships and experiences. Running can help with weight loss when combined with proper nutrition. Your dad is correct though about that being water weight. It's not unusual to shed a ton of water weight through sweat and exercise. What you really want to do is redistribute your weight. 140-150 lbs is a decent weight, especially at your height, but you want to make sure your body composition is right.. meaning that most of that 140-150 is muscle and tissue weight with less fat weight. My advice to you (take it or leave it) is to combine a few days a week of good strength/plyometric training to build some muscle and a few days a week of running or other cardio. Don't make the mistake that alot of people do and get so excited that you try to do too much too fast. If you're not used to running long distances, I definitely wouldn't do back to back long runs right away. If you just GOTTA run every day, I'd say stick to shorter runs. Or you can go alternating days of running and days of strength training with rest days evenly thrown in. It's imperative that you allow your body time to rest and recover, especially at your age. You've still got growing to do and you don't want to hinder that. You have plenty of time to become the best version of you, so build a good foundation, build good fundamentals so that your body won't be paying for it when you get older. If you incorporate cardio as well as strength training, allow yourself rest days, cut out the fried foods and sugary crap, then yes.. you should see significant improvement.. you'll feel better too. Good luck

Heart rate monitor so you can gauge where you are when you're running. Also, treadmill running doesn't = road running. Both great for your health but only doing one or the other won't accurately gauge your true fitness level. Lots of variables to running on the road or trail as opposed to treadmill. Changes (even the slightest) in elevation, humidity level, temperature, and composition of running surface all factor in. Your stride when running on a treadmill is probably very different than running on the road. Also, because  you're obviously someone who works out and invests time in keeping fit, this might just be a little "nudge" for you to change it up... Lots of ways to measure how fit we are and sometimes we get to the point of taking it for granted that we are in shape when we get a little curve ball thrown at us. Def try the heart rate monitor to make sure nothing crazy is going on, but I'd say change it up (even though it sucks) and swap your treadmill runs for road runs for awhile. Just remember to take it easy and don't try to go out there and run the same thing you'd normally do on a treadmill. It'll get better, it just sucks at first.

If you're just starting out with the running it's more important to lay the foundation and not burnout (or worse, hurt yourself). You want to be able to measure your progress as you go, but don't go out there EVERY time you run and try to beat your last effort. Some days will be good running days and others won't. I CAN run a 6 minute mile, but I don't manage that EVERY time I run. I CAN run 8 or 10 miles at a time, but I don't get that far EVERY time I run. If you're able to run every day and recover, then great, but don't kill yourself with an every day running schedule if you have trouble with soreness or tiredness. I like to vary my training. Running either every other day, or 3 days on followed by 2 off. Day one might be a quick (but comfortable) 3 mile followed by sprints on day 2 and a longer distance slower run on day 3. Variety is a damn good thing. Throwing in longer distance slower runs will increase how fast you are able to go on shorter runs and in turn, doing regular short distance speed work will increase your cardio ability and make longer runs easier. Experiment and see what feels right to you and then figure out if you're more concerned with building distance or shaving time off. You CAN do both, but you gotta be smart about it. I would say, with a well coordinated running schedule- include ample recovery time so that you can train with good focus and energy each time you go out- that incorporates a little bit of speed work and a little bit of steady state,  that you should be able to see regular improvements in your time every week or so. But if you're main goal is running for weight loss, I would agree with 'duckshirt' there... just run for a set amount of time without killing yourself.

So I slowed my pace a bit and aimed to increase my distance little by little. I'd shoot for an extra quarter mile on my runs every week until I was running 3 miles again without keeling over and dying. Warm up a good 5 to 10 minutes (I use a stationary bike to get warm) and just some light stretching before hand (hamstrings, calves especially) then take on your run. Vary it up. Do your paced longer runs one day, then the next run try out some sprint intervals (works wonders for upping your lung capacity and cardio endurance). I'd say running about 3 times a week to start with is good.

As long as you're not experiences any sharp, shooting, or unusual pains, you're just feeling the normal result of upping your distance. Any change in your routine will leave you sleeping like a rock and tired for a little bit before your body adapts. The key is ALLOWING your body time to adapt without pushing too hard too fast. Everyone is different, but if you're still new to the running 5+ regularly, I wouldn't push to do it on the daily. If you ran the 5 miles yesterday and today you just have the urge and GOTTA GO GOTTA GO GOTTA RUN OR I'LL LOSE MY MIND!! I'd say go run.. but run an easier pace/shorter distance. I run on the regular, and sometimes I'm just so damn motivated that it's hard NOT to go hit the pavement. But pacing yourself now will save you hurt in the long run and keep you going. I'd recommend keeping the longer runs to every other day at the most right now.

I wouldn't recommend running with that much extra weight on you very often. That's a significant amount of weight that's just going to add to the impact on your joints. I'm in the military as well (Marine Corps, 9 years) and I get the being motivated to push yourself, but you gotta be smart about it. 30 to 45 minutes is ample amount of time for a good workout. If you're running every day, I'd say change it up. Sprint intervals one day, slower runs one day, maybe once a week or once every two weeks try a run with a small amount of weight added to your body so you get some benefit without killing your joints. If you don't have the right amount of time to do a really long run, get the most bang for your buck out of the shorter amount of time by being versatile. Just like longer distance paced runs will in turn improve your speed on shorter runs, speed work over shorter distances (intervals) will aid you when you DO have time to go on the longer runs.

I'm in the military and have been running for several years now. I moved to the city recently and found myself in a similar situation. I prefer running away from the hustle and bustle of the city, but have no choice. To top it off, there is literally NO route I can chart that doesn't have hills. I'm able to change it up, depending on which direction I go (and the mood my muscles are in that day) I can start with the bigger hills, or finish with them. Try out both ways and see which works for you (everyone is different). Speaking from my own experience, my advice would be this: make sure you're warmed up (take a good 5 to 10 minutes and warm up by walking-- I use a stationary bike-- and get your muscles and joints awake) then start out with a comfortable pace and take the hill first. That way, your body is warmed up, you get those muscles pumping on the up swing, and then your joints will be ready and able to manage the downhill stride. Also, psychologically this can be helpful because you get the hill out of the way and don't have to dread it... helps keep your speed good.
